sections.content: For each of the thirteen tasks, this appendix shows three instances under the default visual setting: the prompt excerpt, the rendered image inputs, the ground-truth answer, and the parsed answer from each of eight primary models (Qwen3.5-27B, Gemma4-31B, GLM-4.6V-Flash, Kimi-VL-A3B, GPT-5, Grok-4.20, Gemini-3-Flash, Gemini-3.1-Pro), marked / for correct/incorrect. Shared conventions. For voxel tasks, each block is unit cube at an integer lattice position, with defining the vertical direction. Labels are computed from object coordinates and assigned colors. Each physical block contributes once to an object-level count, even when it appears in both query views. Color categories are the twelve names specified in the prompts, rather than shading variations. The definitions below state each tasks target and label convention; the examples show the default condition. 56 D.1 T1: Volume T1 belongs to the Aggregate quantity and support group (Figure 1). Given two views of one object, the target is the total number of occupied voxel positions, which also gives its volume in cubic block units. Each block counts once, regardless of how many faces or views show it. The hidden-block filter is designed to make each voxel visible in at least one view (Appendix C.1); combining the views therefore requires avoiding duplicate counts while retaining blocks seen in only one. The default response is an integer; the multiple-choice control presents candidate totals for the same target. . . . Your task is to count the total number of blocks that make up the 3D object. . . Given two object views and three container dimensions, the target is whether the object fits under an axis-aligned reorientation. Each object extent is the maximum occupied coordinate minus the minimum plus one. The label is true if any permutation of the three extents is no larger than the corresponding container dimensions, allowing equality. Mental rotation thus changes which object axis aligns with each container axis; the label procedure does not test arbitrary oblique rotations. Unlike T1, this judgment depends on the objects extents rather than its total block count. . . . Your task is to determine whether the object can fit in the boundary in any possible orientation. sections.content: This appendix lists the exact prompt templates used for each task under both inference modes. For Thinking, we use task-specific decomposition instructions that make relevant intermediate reasoning steps explicit, giving models strong, task-appropriate opportunity to solve each task. Non-Thinking simply uses the concise task prompt. Placeholders in double braces (e.g. {{box_dims}}) are filled at inference time. In the Thinking prompts, hidden blocks primarily refers to blocks occluded in one view but recoverable from the other. The independent ambiguity audit identified one evaluated object containing nearly fully occluded block (Appendix C.1). Response-format examples. The examples included in the prompt templates serve only to illustrate the required output structure, including field names, data types, and serialization format. They are not paired with input images and do not constitute worked examples or few-shot demonstrations of the benchmark tasks. Their numerical values are randomly picked by the author for illustrative purposes rather than sampled from the benchmarks ground-truth distribution, and therefore need not satisfy task-specific constraints. For evaluation, each model prediction is scored against the ground truth computed independently by the procedural generator. F.1 T1: Volume (Open-Ended) (cid:215) Non-Thinking You are given two perspective images of the same 3D object from different viewing angles. Your task is to count the total number of blocks that make up the 3D object. Please answer in this format: { total_blocks: int, } Example: { total_blocks: 10, } Thinking You are given two perspective images of the same 3D object from different viewing angles. Your task is to count the total number of blocks that make up the 3D object. Instructions: Analyze the two 3D views: Carefully examine the objects geometry, including visible cubes/blocks, edges, faces, and overlaps. Identify protrusions, stacked structures, and hidden parts that may not be fully visible in one view. Use both perspectives to infer depth and layering. Reconstruct the 3D structure: Combine information from both views to mentally reconstruct the full 3D arrangement. Determine how blocks are stacked along width (X), depth (Y), and height (Z). Pay attention to partially occluded blocks that may only appear in one view. Account for hidden blocks: Some blocks may be hidden behind others in one or both views. Use consistency between the two perspectives to infer missing or occluded blocks. Ensure structural validity (e.g., no floating blocks unless clearly supported). Count the blocks: Count all visible and inferred hidden blocks. Avoid double-counting blocks seen in both views. Ensure every counted block has valid position in the reconstructed 3D structure. Verify consistency: Double-check that your counted structure matches both given perspectives. Ensure all visible features in both images are explained by your reconstruction. Output Format: Please answer in this format: { total_blocks: int, } 118 Example: { total_blocks: 10, } F.2 T1: Volume (MCQ) (cid:215) Non-Thinking You are given two perspective images of the same 3D object from different viewing angles. Your task is to count the total number of blocks that make up the 3D object. Choose the correct answer from the options below: - {{option_1_number}} - {{option_2_number}} - {{option_3_number}} - {{option_4_number}} - {{option_5_number}} Please answer in this format: { total_blocks: int, } Example: { total_blocks: 10, } Note: Your answer must be one of the provided options. Do not output the option index, but the number itself. Thinking You are given two perspective images of the same 3D object from different viewing angles. Your task is to count the total number of blocks that make up the 3D object. Instructions: Analyze the two 3D views: Carefully examine the objects geometry, including visible cubes/blocks, edges, faces, and overlaps. Identify protrusions, stacked structures, and hidden parts that may not be fully visible in one view. Use both perspectives to infer depth and layering. Reconstruct the 3D structure: Combine information from both views to mentally reconstruct the full 3D arrangement. Determine how blocks are stacked along width (X), depth (Y), and height (Z). Pay attention to partially occluded blocks that may only appear in one view. Account for hidden blocks: Some blocks may be hidden behind others in one or both views. Use consistency between the two perspectives to infer missing or occluded blocks. Ensure structural validity (e.g., no floating blocks unless clearly supported). Count the blocks: Count all visible and inferred hidden blocks. Avoid double-counting blocks seen in both views. Ensure every counted block has valid position in the reconstructed 3D structure. Verify consistency: Double-check that your counted structure matches both given perspectives. Ensure all visible features in both images are explained by your reconstruction. Choose the correct answer from the options below: - {{option_1_number}} - {{option_2_number}} - {{option_3_number}} - {{option_4_number}} - {{option_5_number}} Output Format: Please answer in this format: 119 { total_blocks: int, } Example: { total_blocks: 10, } Note: Your answer must be one of the provided options. Do not output the option index, but the number itself. F.3 T2: Packaging (cid:215) Non-Thinking You are given two perspective images of the same 3D object from different viewing angles, along with 3D boundary defined by its dimensions. Your task is to determine whether the object can fit in the boundary in any possible orientation. Boundary: {{box_dims}} Please answer in this format: { answer: boolean, } Example: { answer: true, } Thinking You are given two perspective images of the same 3D object from different viewing angles, along with 3D boundary defined by its dimensions. Your task is to determine whether the object can fit in the boundary in any possible orientation. Instructions: Analyze the two 3D views: Carefully examine the objects geometry, including its overall shape, dimensions, and structure. Identify key features such as length, width, height, protrusions, and irregularities. Use both perspectives to understand the full extent of the object in 3D space. Reconstruct the 3D structure: Mentally reconstruct the object using information from both views. Estimate the objects dimensions along the three axes (X, Y, Z). Consider the maximum extents of the object in each direction. Understand the boundary constraints: The boundary is defined by three dimensions (e.g., length, width, height). Treat the boundary as rectangular box. The object must fit entirely in this box without exceeding any dimension. Consider all possible orientations: The object can be rotated freely. Check all permutations of the objects dimensions against the boundary dimensions. Determine if there exists at least one orientation where all object dimensions are less than or equal to the corresponding boundary dimensions. Make the decision: If the object fits within the boundary in at least one orientation -> it is valid. If the object cannot fit in any orientation -> it is invalid. Boundary: {{box_dims}} Output Format: Please answer in this format: { answer: boolean, } 120 Example: { answer: true, } F.4 T3: Difference (cid:215) Non-Thinking You are given four perspective images representing two different 3D objects (two views per object). Your task is to analyze both objects and determine the difference in their block compositions. Please answer in this format: { answer_intersection: int, answer_only_a: int, answer_only_b: int, } Example: { answer_intersection: 2, answer_only_a: 4, answer_only_b: 5, } Note: answer_intersection is the number of shared blocks, answer_only_a is the number of blocks that only appears in the first two images, answer_only_b is the number of blocks that only appears in the last two images. Thinking You are given four perspective images representing two different 3D objects (two views per object). Your task is to analyze both objects and determine the difference in their block compositions. Instructions: Group the views: The input consists of 4 images include 2 views correspond to Object and 2 views correspond to Object B. Correctly group the images so that each pair represents the same object. Analyze each object separately: For each object, examine its two views carefully. Identify visible blocks, structure, stacking, and spatial layout. Infer hidden or occluded blocks using both views. Reconstruct the 3D structures: Mentally reconstruct Object and Object in 3D. Determine the position of each block in terms of width (X), depth (Y), and height (Z). Ensure consistency between the two views of each object. Count the blocks: Count the total number of blocks in Object A. Count the total number of blocks in Object B. Avoid doublecounting blocks visible in both views. Compute the differences: Identify blocks that exist in both objects (shared structure). Identify blocks that exist only in Object A. Identify blocks that exist only in Object B. Verify consistency: Ensure that all counted blocks are consistent with the given views. Check that differences are logically derived from the reconstructed structures. sections.title: H Use of AI Assistants
sections.content: We used AI coding and writing assistants (Claude Code and ChatGPT/Codex) in three ways. For coding, they helped write and refactor the data generator, evaluation harness, probing code, analysis and plotting scripts, and the release package. For writing, they helped revise the wording and structure of drafts written by the authors and check that numbers in the text, tables, and figures were consistent. For literature search, they helped locate candidate related papers. The authors designed the study and experiments, read every cited paper, and checked all generated code and text. Every number in the paper was recomputed by scripts from the saved model outputs, and the authors take full responsibility for the content. The models evaluated in this paper are research objects and were not used as assistants.
